articles.title: Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
articles.summary: Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this…
articles.abstract: Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.

articles.title: Multi-Objective Evolutionary Semi-Supervised Learning for Resource-Aware Smart City Classification
articles.summary: Smart-city applications often combine scarce labeled data with abundant unlabeled observations. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) exploits both labeled and unlabeled data to improve classification under…
articles.abstract: Smart-city applications often combine scarce labeled data with abundant unlabeled observations. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) exploits both labeled and unlabeled data to improve classification under limited supervision. This article presents MOEA-SSL, a multi-objective evolutionary approach for lightweight semi-supervised tabular classification that jointly optimizes predictive quality and feature usage. Experimental evaluation on three Smart City classification datasets, considering 1\%, 5\%, and 10\% labeled data, shows that MOEA-SSL achieves competitive predictive performance compared with established lightweight SSL methods while significantly reducing feature usage relative to EA-SSL in all evaluated conditions. The computed Pareto fronts also provide lower-feature-use alternatives with limited degradation in classification performance.

articles.title: Is Anyone Enforcing the Cartel? What Reinforcement Learning Teaches LLM Agents in Markets
articles.summary: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits,…
articles.abstract: Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

articles.title: Exact Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Polynomial Expected Queries
articles.summary: Envy-free cake cutting asks how to divide a resource so that no agent prefers another agent's share. Finding such a division with few queries about preferences has been a longstanding challenge.
articles.abstract: Envy-free cake cutting asks how to divide a resource so that no agent prefers another agent's share. Finding such a division with few queries about preferences has been a longstanding challenge. Aziz and Mackenzie gave the first query bound depending only on the number $n$ of agents: a tower of six $n$'s. Subsequent improvements culminated in Ye and Bai's single-exponential bound of $n^{O(1)}2^n$. A large gap remains between this deterministic upper bound and Procaccia's general lower bound of $Ω(n^2)$. Whether polynomially many queries suffice is a central open question in fair division. We show that a polynomial expected query bound is possible. Our randomised protocol uses only independent, uniformly sampled points from the cake as its source of randomness. For every profile of $n$ agents with nonnegative, additive, nonatomic valuations, the protocol has the following guarantees: (1) It terminates with probability one. (2) Every allocation it returns is complete and exactly envy-free. (3) Its expected number of Robertson-Webb queries is $\widetilde{O}(n^{30})$. The expectation is taken solely over the protocol's random choices, with no distributional assumptions on preferences.

articles.title: Subjective Valuations Make It Hard to be Fair: The Complexity of Resource Allocation to Groups of Agents
articles.summary: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not…
articles.abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of finding an EF1 allocation of indivisible items in the group-sharing setting, which has received increasing attention in recent years. There, items are not allocated to individual agents but rather to one of two (or possibly more) groups, and agents within that group all share the assigned items. We consider both the "fixed" (EF1-Fix) and "variable" (EF1-Var) group cases, where in the former the assignments of agents to groups are prescribed. While both are NP-hard in the classical sense, we show that their algorithmic behavior differs significantly from the parameterized perspective. As our main results, we: (1) prove that both cases are NP-hard even when the number of agents is a small constant; (2) circumvent this hardness by establishing fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Var w.r.t. the number of "subjective" items, that is, items which are viewed as chores or goods by different agents---but rule out an analogous result for EF1-Fix; and (3) establish fixed-parameter tractability for EF1-Fix w.r.t. the number of item types, but link the existence of an analogous fixed-parameter algorithm for EF1-Var to a fundamental open question in the setting of Integer Linear Programming.

articles.title: Best-of-Both Worlds Proportionality in Structured Committee Elections
articles.summary: We study randomized committee elections with additive preferences, where we seek best-of-both-worlds proportionality. That is, we strive for strong guarantees for the selection probabilities ex ante…
articles.abstract: We study randomized committee elections with additive preferences, where we seek best-of-both-worlds proportionality. That is, we strive for strong guarantees for the selection probabilities ex ante and each realized committee ex post. We focus on structured preferences and introduce antichain single-peakedness, a restricted domain generalizing single-peaked additive preferences as well as several well-studied approval domains. Our approach first computes a fractional committee and then decomposes it through a rounding rule called systematic rounding. Among profile-oblivious rounding rules, we characterize systematic rounding as the unique rule satisfying natural quota guarantees, and thereby the only promising rule for our two-step approach. We show that ex-ante core stability is incompatible with ex-post justified representation $JR$, even under single-peaked preferences. However, applying systematic rounding to certain fractional allocations that form so-called Lindahl equilibria yields ex-ante core stability and ex-post core stability up to one. Alternatively, we retain exact ex-post proportionality and approximate the ex-ante core using two parameters: $α$ raises the utility gain required for a deviation, while $β$ reduces the coalition's proportional share. We establish the tight threshold $αβ$=2. Below it, ex-post JR is incompatible even under single-peaked preferences; at and above it, adapting a fractional rule called BestRepresentative [Pierczyński and Skowron, 2022] and applying systematic rounding to its output yields ex-ante $α, β$-fractional core stability and ex-post PJR under antichain single-peaked preferences.

articles.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria
articles.summary: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional…
articles.abstract: We show that computing an approximate correlated equilibrium of a polytope game is PPAD-complete, and thus polynomial-time equivalent to finding a Nash equilibrium. This challenges the conventional view in game theory that correlated equilibria are more tractable objects than Nash equilibria. From a conceptual standpoint, we connect correlated equilibria to a natural generalization of fixed points, which we call fixed sets. A fixed set of a continuous function $f$ is a nonempty finite set $S$ such that $S \subseteq \operatorname{conv} f(S)$. Our main technical contribution is to prove that computing a fixed set is PPAD-hard even at inverse polynomial precision.

articles.title: Splitting Planar Necklaces with Few Straight Cuts
articles.summary: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the…
articles.abstract: In the classical necklace splitting problem, beads of different colors lie on a line, and the goal is to divide them among $k$ agents using as few cuts as possible so that every agent receives the same number of beads of each color. We study the planar analog in which a cut is a full straight line and the objective is minimizing the number of lines: $m$ points colored red and blue must be separated by straight-line cuts into regions that can be allocated to $k$ agents so that each agent receives the same number of points of each color. Projection to a line gives $2(k-1)$ cuts, and $k-1$ are sometimes necessary; we give algorithms, static and dynamic, that provably close part of this gap. We develop several approaches that capitalize on the extra degree of freedom: a ``star'' search that produces solutions with as few as $\lceil \frac{k}{2} \rceil$ cuts and never more than $k$ whenever a fair contiguous circular partition exists, with further guarantees for evenly spaced input, and a general algorithm that produces at most $k + \log_2(k+1) - 2$ cuts in $Θ(m \log k)$ time, built on a one-dimensional necklace splitting subroutine that requires no presorting. We then adapt the general algorithm to a dynamic setting, maintaining exact fairness and the cut bound under arbitrary relocation of points, with expected update time that scales with the total distance moved.

articles.title: Extending Mechanisms
articles.summary: Given an incentive-compatible mechanism for a single agent on a restricted domain of valuations, we consider its incentive-compatible extensions to the entire valuation space. We identify two extreme…
articles.abstract: Given an incentive-compatible mechanism for a single agent on a restricted domain of valuations, we consider its incentive-compatible extensions to the entire valuation space. We identify two extreme extensions: the "keep-the-menu" extension, which minimizes buyer payoffs and maximizes canonical prices pointwise, and the "keep-the-pricing" extension, which maximizes buyer payoffs and minimizes canonical prices pointwise.

articles.title: Evaluating Spiking MoveNet Deployability for Near-Future Onboard Spiking Satellite Pose Estimation
articles.summary: SNNs are attracting interest due to their potential for energy efficiency and event-driven processing. However, neuromorphic hardware is not yet mature enough to enable embedded deployment of complex…
articles.abstract: SNNs are attracting interest due to their potential for energy efficiency and event-driven processing. However, neuromorphic hardware is not yet mature enough to enable embedded deployment of complex spiking network architectures. In this work, we investigate a spiking version of the MoveNet architecture tailored for autonomous spacecraft operation, aiming to evaluate the deployability of this complex architecture compared to the non-spiking version for embedded, fully event-based solutions in space applications. Using the RAPTOR dataset, we compare the performance and operational cost of the proposed S-MoveNet-Lightning architecture with its standard version, MoveNet-Lightning. Our results show balanced advantages in computational resources and architectural settings for spiking U-Net-like architectures. An evaluation of the performance and hardware footprint of the proposed Spiking Neural Network (SNN) approach for pose estimation shows that, on average, 2.2 times fewer multiplication and accumulation operations are required compared to the non-spiking solution deployed on FPGA platforms with the AMD Deep Learning Processor Unit (DPU). These results provide valuable insights into the feasibility and potential of SNNs in complex aerospace applications and highlight their role in balancing efficiency and performance, paving the way for event-driven solutions in embedded space applications.

articles.title: Hybrid metaheuristics for architectural design optimization under small evaluation and wall-clock budgets
articles.summary: Architectural and structural design optimization in parametric software affords about a thousand evaluations of an expensive model for problems with tens of variables, a regime for which most…
articles.abstract: Architectural and structural design optimization in parametric software affords about a thousand evaluations of an expensive model for problems with tens of variables, a regime for which most metaheuristics were not designed. On the side of artificial intelligence, two hybrid metaheuristics are proposed: a covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) whose sampling is enriched with differential-evolution trial vectors, and a particle swarm with success-history parameter adaptation, differential-evolution injection and local refinement. A budget-aware delay of population-size reduction in adaptive differential evolution is also proposed. Under a hard cap of 1,200 evaluations, all counted, the CMA-ES hybrid ranks first on seven shifted and rotated functions at 10 and 30 variables and beats CMA-ES on six of seven functions at 30 variables. Ablations attribute this gain to the injection and show that a local search pays off only when its result re-enters the population. The delayed schedule improves three adaptive differential-evolution variants in 40 of 51 comparisons, with no loss. On the side of engineering application, in Grasshopper the CMA-ES hybrid and plain CMA-ES are never significantly worse than the optimizers of Galapagos, SilverEye, Opossum and Tunny on travelling-salesman instances and on a built 85-variable free-form shell, where they end 48 % below the best external tool in 15 minutes. On a 22-variable building-performance problem with binary choices, differential evolution leads instead. Shifting and rotating the functions reverses the rank of Harris hawks optimization. Solvers should therefore be selected by problem structure and stopping time, not by a single ranking.

articles.title: A Spiking Ring-Attractor Architecture for Representation and Control of Revolute Robot Joints
articles.summary: Robotic systems with revolute joints evolve on circular state spaces, yet most control architectures represent these states using Euclidean variables that ignore this underlying geometry. We propose…
articles.abstract: Robotic systems with revolute joints evolve on circular state spaces, yet most control architectures represent these states using Euclidean variables that ignore this underlying geometry. We propose a fully spiking neural control architecture in which ring attractors encode joint states, enforcing representations consistent with the topology of revolute systems. Homeostatic regulation computes goal-state mismatch directly over these distributed representations, and opponent gain-modulated populations convert this mismatch into controlled phase shifts of the activity bump, implementing set-point regulation as motion on the ring. We show that the bump dynamics follow an SO(2) geometry, and that gain asymmetries induce a signed phase velocity on the ring. To interface distributed activity with scalar regulation signals, we derive an analytic Fourier phase decoder and implement its signed components using push-pull spiking populations. For multi-joint systems, we demonstrate that local ring-based Fourier features compose into product representations that linearly decode SO(3) orientations through forward kinematics. Experiments in NEST validate the full SO(2) regulation mechanism and the spiking product-feature decoder for lift, pitch, and yaw. Robot experiments on a Tiago arm show that decoded ring dynamics generate joint velocity commands, producing directed motion with joint-dependent accuracy. Together, these results establish a neuromorphic control framework in which representation, regulation, and action are unified within a ring-attractor substrate aligned with the geometry of revolute systems.

articles.title: Sector-Ring Linear Reservoirs: Sector-Wise Decay-Timescale Allocation With State Reuse Across Candidate Settings
articles.summary: In reservoir computing, performance depends on whether the fixed dynamics of the reservoir suit the task, and the appropriate memory length and frequency response differ across tasks. The reservoir…
articles.abstract: In reservoir computing, performance depends on whether the fixed dynamics of the reservoir suit the task, and the appropriate memory length and frequency response differ across tasks. The reservoir settings are found by a search on each task, and driving the reservoir with the input and collecting its states for every candidate setting dominates the cost of the search. In a reservoir with a linear recurrence, the dynamics decompose into modes, one per eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue distribution becomes a design variable. We propose the Sector-Ring Linear Reservoir (SRLR), in which the eigenvalue angles are fixed at evenly spaced positions around a circle and one decay timescale, chosen from a few values, is assigned to each sector of consecutive angles. To keep the scale of each mode's state equal across candidates, the input weights are scaled using the power spectrum of the training input. To reduce the cost of the search, the states of the modes for each decay-timescale value are computed once and reused across candidates. On prediction and reconstruction benchmarks built from chaotic systems, the SRLR achieved, in all eight cases, a lower mean test error than a reference model in which all modes share one decay timescale, and was competitive with nonlinear echo state network and leaky-integrator echo state network baselines. The selected decay-timescale profiles changed with the prediction target and horizon. The state reuse reduced the number of computed mode trajectories in the search by 99.8% relative to per-candidate recomputation.

articles.title: Migrate Computation, Not Data: Fault Recovery in Neuromorphic Many-Core Systems
articles.summary: As neuromorphic systems scale to thousands of near-memory cores, aging-induced permanent faults in neuron-update datapaths become an important obstacle to long-term deployment. Existing online…
articles.abstract: As neuromorphic systems scale to thousands of near-memory cores, aging-induced permanent faults in neuron-update datapaths become an important obstacle to long-term deployment. Existing online recovery methods typically retire a faulty core and migrate its neurons, along with their weights and membrane states, to healthy cores. This whole-core treatment incurs high recovery traffic and makes recovery depend on scarce destinations; at high utilization, there may be enough surviving compute capacity but insufficient free storage to copy the affected neuron context. This paper presents SpikeRelay, an online recovery framework for diagnosed compute-unit faults. SpikeRelay exploits the fact that, in many neuromorphic cores, the compute datapath, local SRAM, and router are distinct modules: a compute fault need not destroy stored weights and states or disconnect the core from the NoC. Instead of retiring a faulty core and migrating its neuron data, SpikeRelay converts the faulty core into a storage-and-forwarding node while offloading neuron-update computation to a healthy rescue core. This decoupling of storage and computation eliminates recovery-time data migration and greatly reduces spare-SRAM requirements. Consequently, SpikeRelay sustains 100\% recovery at 92.2\% SRAM utilization and a 50\% fault rate, whereas the best baseline achieves only 22.1\%.

articles.title: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks
articles.summary: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed…
articles.abstract: Trust and reputation mechanisms can reduce the influence of malicious clients in federated learning (FL), but strict update filtering is difficult under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data because honest local updates may temporarily reduce performance on a shared validation proxy. Extending an earlier trust-based semi-decentralized FL (SDFL) framework, this paper operationalizes the trust signals and introduces peer-relative update screening that combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality. The method is evaluated with 50 MNIST clients, 20% persistent label-flip attackers, Dirichlet heterogeneity levels of 0.5 and 0.1, 100 communication rounds, and five paired random seeds. Under moderate heterogeneity, the proposed method reaches 98.37% final accuracy while rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates and retaining 90.30% of benign updates; the final benign and malicious trust distributions are completely separated (KS=1.00). Under severe heterogeneity, it reaches 95.25% accuracy, rejects 88.55% of malicious updates, and retains 76.90% of benign updates (KS=0.96). Trust weighting alone preserves slightly higher utility in the most heterogeneous condition, but accepts all malicious submissions. The results therefore distinguish influence mitigation from explicit containment and quantify the utility-selectivity trade-off introduced by screening. The study provides an empirically validated off-chain governance core that can feed blockchain-based audit and incentive layers in SDFL.

articles.title: Let Them Sleep: Recursive Self-Pruning Memory for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
articles.summary: Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working…
articles.abstract: Agents that run for a long time have a memory problem, and it is not the one most systems optimize for. Storing every trace and retrieving the nearest neighbors works early and quietly stops working later: the store fills up with failures the agent then repeats, and with facts that were true fifty turns ago. RSPM (Recursive Self-Pruning Memory) borrows the fix biology already found. At intervals the agent sleeps. It clusters its recent failures, distills each cluster into a short rule, and deletes the raw episodes it just learned from. Rules decay unless something reinforces them, and rules that recur across many contexts get promoted into general ones. We tested this on three settings with little in common: a difficulty-calibrated SWE-bench simulation, temporal consistency across 12 conversational benchmarks, and long-horizon QA on LoCoMo-10. All three improve, by 9.1, 11.9, and 7.6 points respectively. More interestingly, the two studies that instrument the store itself converge on nearly the same operating point without being tuned toward it: roughly 93% fewer retry loops and roughly 30% fewer stored entries. That hints that knowing what to forget is a general property of agent memory rather than a benchmark-specific trick.

articles.title: Small-scale neural simulation of Caenorhabditis elegans on Loihi-2 using NeuroML2Loihi
articles.summary: Neural simulation is an essential methodology for studying biological nervous systems, but it remains limited by the computational costs of repeatedly updating neural and synaptic states over many…
articles.abstract: Neural simulation is an essential methodology for studying biological nervous systems, but it remains limited by the computational costs of repeatedly updating neural and synaptic states over many timesteps. Neuromorphic hardware is a promising substrate for this class of workloads because such devices combine event-driven execution, localized memory, and spike-based communication. However, neuromorphic \textit{software} remains comparatively fragmented and difficult to integrate with the model-description standards used by the computational neuroscience community. This disconnect limits reproducible experimentation and makes direct comparison between conventional and neuromorphic simulation workflows difficult. This paper introduces ``NeuroML2Loihi'', an open-source framework for translating NeuroML model descriptions into Loihi~2-deployable Lava primitives, enabling standardized biological models to be executed on Intel's Loihi~2 neuromorphic chip. We evaluate our framework using c302-derived \textit{C. elegans} neural models across three connectome-scale configurations. Cross-platform similarity is assessed using spike-train and voltage-trace metrics, while latency, power, and energy consumption are benchmarked against the conventional reference workflow. Across the evaluated models, Loihi~2 execution enabled through NeuroML2Loihi achieves 514--1211$\times$ lower latency and a 1.8--1.9$\times$ reduction in mean wattage relative to the NEURON reference, producing substantially lower total energy consumption primarily through reduced execution time. These results demonstrate that standards-based neuromorphic neural simulation is feasible on Loihi~2 and can support meaningful comparison against established computational neuroscience workflows.

articles.title: Length-Independent Stability and $L_2$-Gain Certificates for Chains of Delayed Neural Modules
articles.summary: Networks of repeated neural modules with delayed neighbour coupling need stability guarantees for every number of modules, but delay-dependent criteria certify one network at a time and grow with its…
articles.abstract: Networks of repeated neural modules with delayed neighbour coupling need stability guarantees for every number of modules, but delay-dependent criteria certify one network at a time and grow with its size. This paper derives stability and $L_2$-gain certificates of length-independent size for open chains and rings of modules of two alternating types with slope-restricted activations. A local and a transmission delay act independently and are only bounded and continuous. A Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional with fixed integration limits and module-local variables that repeat with the module type reduces the certificate of every chain to one cell of two modules. Local conditions and a single linear matrix inequality of order 96 on this cell, or 104 for the gain, certify global asymptotic stability and a common $L_2$-gain bound for all open chains and all rings with an even number of at least four modules. Up to a margin, the stability inequality is also necessary for the repeated variables to certify every length. All uniform certificates, including certified coupling regions, are verified in exact rational arithmetic. In the numerical study, the certified coupling reaches 92% of an outer bound given by unstable members of the model class for short delays and 79% at the nominal delay bounds. For 16 modules at unit coupling strength, certificates of the same functional computed for that length alone raise the certified delay scale by 2% to 7% in four cases. A single stability problem with 1298 scalar variables thus replaces per-length certification of long chains at little cost.

articles.title: Organon : From Evolutionary Search to Recursive Self-Improving Agents for Scientific Discovery
articles.summary: Scientific discovery does not follow a single fixed methodology: research methods vary across domains and evolve through experimentation as investigations unfold. Although LLM-guided evolutionary…
articles.abstract: Scientific discovery does not follow a single fixed methodology: research methods vary across domains and evolve through experimentation as investigations unfold. Although LLM-guided evolutionary search has advanced automated discovery, existing frameworks typically rely on fixed search procedures or restrict adaptation to predefined components, limiting their ability to address diverse research problems and adapt to challenges that emerge at runtime. We introduce Organon, a recursively self-improving agent for scientific discovery. During execution, a single persistent agent analyzes its accumulated experience and autonomously revises its own search strategies, population management, diagnostic tools, memory, and worker coordination. These revisions take effect at runtime, allowing the agent to continuously adapt its approach as research progresses. Importantly, the agent can also diagnose and correct flaws in its own adaptation procedures, enabling recursive improvement of the mechanisms that guide its future self-improvement. We evaluate Organon across 21 computational discovery tasks spanning algorithm design, GPU kernel optimization, mathematical construction, and systems optimization. On ALE-Bench Lite, Organon achieves the best performance among competing search frameworks on all 10 tasks, improving mean held-out performance by 20.5% over EvoX. On KernelBench, it achieves the best results on three of four workloads, with speedups of up to 1.67x over the strongest competing method. Analysis of the search trajectories further reveals how the agent develops task-specific search strategies, builds new diagnostic capabilities, and corrects or reverses its own earlier revisions. We implement Organon using DeepSeek Harness and Cordis's spatiotemporal composability. Code is available at https://github.com/cheikh025/Organon.

articles.title: QD-Rec: Open-Ended Evolution of Recommendations via Quality-Diversity
articles.summary: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to…
articles.abstract: Open-ended search combined with foundation models has produced advances such as faster algorithms, new results on open mathematical problems, and self-improving agents. We extend this paradigm to recommendation for decision-making, focusing on decisions where the set of possible choices is fixed but the reasons for choosing them are not. In high-stakes decisions, e.g., which company to acquire or which customer to target, comparing diverse, well-reasoned options can be more useful than a single ranked list. We formalize open-ended recommendation as building a diverse, high-quality set of recommendations, each an item together with a hypothesis, a natural-language reason why the item fits the needs of a decision maker. We propose QD-Rec, a quality--diversity method that selects items with a contextual bandit and generates hypotheses with a foundation model from earlier ones kept in an archive as stepping stones. A new recommendation enters the archive if it is novel or better than its nearest neighbor. Across M&A, customer targeting, and paper and book recommendation, QD-Rec gives the highest mean quality and builds the largest archive in most settings.

articles.title: Algorithm Modelization: Transforming Optimization Algorithms into Evolvable Intelligence
articles.summary: Can algorithms be learned and evolved as models, rather than repeatedly redesigned as programs? We explore this question by introducing Algorithm Modelization, a new paradigm that turns iterative…
articles.abstract: Can algorithms be learned and evolved as models, rather than repeatedly redesigned as programs? We explore this question by introducing Algorithm Modelization, a new paradigm that turns iterative algorithms into trainable models. Its central idea is to regard algorithm execution trajectories as computational experience: by learning how algorithmic states evolve over iterations, a model can internalize the knowledge embodied in existing algorithms, reproduce their computational behaviors, and further evolve beyond them through training. As a first realization of this paradigm, we modelize iterative optimization as an autoregressive process, where preceding generations constitute the computational context for generating the next population. We develop a dimension-independent population-temporal architecture to capture both population interactions and iterative dynamics, together with an imitation-to-surpassing learning framework that first acquires algorithmic knowledge from heterogeneous teachers and then improves the resulting optimizer directly through optimization feedback. The modelized optimizer consequently goes beyond reproducing individual algorithms: it consolidates heterogeneous search knowledge into a single trainable model, achieves stronger optimization capability through subsequent improvement, and generalizes its acquired knowledge across problems and substantially larger unseen dimensions. More fundamentally, Algorithm Modelization makes algorithmic capability accumulable through learning, where new algorithms and problem-solving experience can become training resources for progressively improving the model. Our results establish a promising path from manually designed algorithms toward general algorithm models that learn, generalize, and evolve from computational experience.

articles.title: Wavelength Diversity Expands the Expressive Power of Optical Computing
articles.summary: Universal function approximation underpins neural networks' capacity to represent nonlinear relationships, but realizing this capability in optical hardware requires engineering the computational…
articles.abstract: Universal function approximation underpins neural networks' capacity to represent nonlinear relationships, but realizing this capability in optical hardware requires engineering the computational features encoded in light. Here, we show that wavelength diversity enhances optical function-approximation expressivity through wavelength-scaled Fourier features generated by a shared phase encoder, without increasing the number of input-encoded harmonics. Multiple wavelengths contribute to the representation of each output function rather than merely serving as independent computational channels. We establish theoretical scaling laws and approximation-error bounds, revealing that, for nondispersive encoders, the spectral endpoints determine the accessible computational bandwidth, while intermediate illumination wavelengths enrich the available harmonics within that bandwidth. Numerical studies demonstrate improved approximation of real- and complex-valued nonlinear functions, with a representative design achieving more than a 100-fold reduction in mean-squared error relative to tested monochromatic optical processors with the same number of trainable phase features. Experimentally, we validate enhanced approximation accuracy and demonstrate the simultaneous approximation of 4,136 distinct nonlinear functions using a compact, single-layer diffractive processor under five-wavelength illumination. These results establish wavelength diversity as an additional physical resource for scaling the expressive power of optical computing and enhancing the accuracy of parallel nonlinear function approximation.

articles.title: SpikeQ: Spike-Guided Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
articles.summary: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and…
articles.abstract: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.

articles.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks
articles.summary: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking…
articles.abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.

articles.title: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems as Scalable and Efficient Physical Neural Networks
articles.summary: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical…
articles.abstract: The rapid growth in the size of state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) models has led to increasing compute demands, spurring the development of energy-efficient hardware accelerators. Physical systems trained to perform ML inference, known as physical neural networks, have been proposed as accelerators in part because of their potential to be highly energy efficient. However, the ML inference accuracies reported in most investigations of physical neural networks have been substantially below the state of the art for conventional digital neural networks. In this work, we show in simulation studies that by applying modern ML training practices, including model compression, various candidate physical neural networks based on nonlinear dynamical systems can achieve accuracies as high as 99.2% on MNIST handwritten-digit recognition. We also show for one dynamical system that using it as the core building block of a parameter-efficient ML architecture inspired by MLP-Mixers enables accuracies of up to 86.4% on CIFAR-10 image classification (92.2% with pretraining and knowledge distillation), compared with 64% for the same system without the mixer architecture. The mixer approach achieved its accuracy while using $>5\times$ fewer trainable parameters than the baseline. Finally, we present back-of-the-envelope estimates for inference energy efficiency and speed when using an example physical dynamical system, suggesting that orders of magnitude improvements may be possible over digital-electronic neural networks.

articles.title: A restart rule for genetic algorithms based on Schnabel census
articles.summary: A new adaptive restart rule for Genetic Algorithms (GAs) is considered. The rule is based on the Schnabel Census method, originally developed for statistical estimation of a size of animal population.
articles.abstract: A new adaptive restart rule for Genetic Algorithms (GAs) is considered. The rule is based on the Schnabel Census method, originally developed for statistical estimation of a size of animal population. In this paper, the Schnabel Census method is applied as a heuristic to estimate the number of different solutions that may be visited with positive probability, given the current distribution of offspring. The rule consists in restarting a GA as soon as the maximum likelihood estimate reaches the number of different solutions observed at the recent iterations. We demonstrate how the new restart rule can be applied in a GA with steady-state replacement scheme, using three different combinatorial optimization problems as examples. Computational experiments on well-known benchmarks show a statistically significant advantage of the GAs with the new restarting rule over the original versions of GAs. The new restart rule also tends to be superior to the well-known rule, which restarts an algorithm when the current iteration number is twice the number of iterations till the current best incumbent was found.

articles.title: Attention over noisy examples: generalization and memorization in the exponential Hopfield network
articles.summary: In Hebbian learning from examples, a Hopfield network retrieves archetypes seen only through noisy examples. We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the…
articles.abstract: In Hebbian learning from examples, a Hopfield network retrieves archetypes seen only through noisy examples. We study it in the exponential Hopfield model: one softmax attention step with the unlabelled examples as keys. A signal-to-noise analysis gives the overlap with an unseen archetype in closed form: a majority-rule law in which an attention entropy replaces the dataset entropy. At high temperature the archetype is lost in the crosstalk; at low temperature the softmax freezes on the closest training example, as in a random energy model, and the layer memorizes. In between, in a window widening with the square root of the network size, the layer pools the examples of the correct class and retrieves the unseen archetype as well as their majority vote allows, at any fixed load. On structured datasets, such as MNIST and fashion-MNIST, the best accuracy lies beyond the freezing.

articles.title: Beyond the Hamming Cliff: Compact Spatial Encodings Preserving Semantic Distance in Spiking Neural Networks
articles.summary: By pre-processing input signals with Gray, Thermometer, Johnson and hybrid encodings before passing them to spiking neural networks running on SpiNNaker hardware, Davies et al.(2025) address the…
articles.abstract: By pre-processing input signals with Gray, Thermometer, Johnson and hybrid encodings before passing them to spiking neural networks running on SpiNNaker hardware, Davies et al.(2025) address the semantic-spatial disparity that causes the ``Hamming cliff'' in standard binary representations. Continuous semantic patterns are presented as a set of simultaneous spikes at the input layer, preserving ultra-low latency processing. Training the network on multiple continuous values under each scheme, and measuring accuracy, required homeostatic scaling and false-positive rates, shows that removing the cliff is necessary but not sufficient: Gray encoding removes it yet retains little global distance structure, whereas Thermometer and Johnson preserve semantic distance at a code width that grows with the value range. The proposed hybrid encodings contain all three as limiting cases of a single parameter, recovering most of that structure at a fraction of the width. The homeostatic factor is shown to set a radius of tolerance around each trained pattern, so that the choice of encoding alone decides which values the network treats as similar.

articles.title: Approaching Backpropagation Accuracy with Weight Perturbation on MNIST
articles.summary: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training…
articles.abstract: Weight perturbation (WP) estimates learning directions from random parameter perturbations and a scalar change in loss, without backpropagating derivatives. We examine how batch size, training duration, and estimator stabilization affect its attainable accuracy in fully connected MNIST networks. In the shallow configuration, large-batch training reaches approximately 97\% test accuracy, compared with an early backpropagation (BP) reference near 97.5--98\%. The same comparison exposes a substantial efficiency gap: under a ten-epoch budget, shallow WP reaches 90.2\%, whereas the reported BP reference reaches 97.4\%. Epoch-indexed curves show diminishing returns from increasing batch size beyond 4,000. Learning-rate reduction and averaging independent perturbation-based updates also stabilize deeper networks, although their recorded results do not establish BP-level accuracy. We distinguish these empirical findings from a finite-horizon approximation argument: under stated regularity conditions, population WP can approximate a fixed gradient-descent trajectory arbitrarily closely at any fixed finite depth. Positive classification margins then suffice to preserve the reference predictions on a finite test set with arbitrarily high probability. Together, the results identify near-BP accuracy as a configuration- and budget-dependent possibility, rather than evidence of equal efficiency or an unconditional accuracy guarantee across depth.

articles.title: First Mathematical Runtime Analyses of Evolutionary Multitask Multi-Objective Optimization
articles.summary: To facilitate the solving of complex problems, evolutionary multitask optimization is regarded as a promising technique due to its capacity for cross-task knowledge transfer. In contrast to empirical…
articles.abstract: To facilitate the solving of complex problems, evolutionary multitask optimization is regarded as a promising technique due to its capacity for cross-task knowledge transfer. In contrast to empirical evidences, no mathematical runtime support exists for this technique within the domain of multi-objective optimization. In this work, we aim to fill this important gap. We analyze how the representative multiobjective multifactorial evolutionary algorithm (MO-MFEA) covers the Pareto fronts of two bi-objective problems simultaneously. For the two-task problem of maximizing the classic bi-objective OMM and the multimodal OJZJ benchmarks, the MO-MFEA requires only an expected runtime of $O(n^2 \log n)$---the same as optimizing the simple OMM alone---yet achieves a speedup by a factor of $Θ(n^{k-1}/\log n)$ compared to optimizing OJZJ alone (with gap size $k$). Similarly, for the task pair comprising the classic LOTZ and the multimodal DLTB benchmarks, a speedup of $Θ(n)$ is attained over optimizing DLTB alone, while the runtime matches that of optimizing LOTZ alone.

articles.title: IWOO: Wave Optics Optimizer Improved with Hybrid Strategies for Numerical Optimization and Engineering Applications
articles.summary: The Wave Optics Optimizer (WOO) incorporates optical diffraction and interference into numerical optimization and has shown competitive performance in benchmarks and engineering applications.…
articles.abstract: The Wave Optics Optimizer (WOO) incorporates optical diffraction and interference into numerical optimization and has shown competitive performance in benchmarks and engineering applications. However, it can converge slowly, become trapped in local optima, and lose search effectiveness in later iterations. This paper proposes an Improved Wave Optics Optimizer (IWOO) that integrates four complementary strategies. First, a good point set and opposition-based learning are combined in GPS--OBL initialization to improve population quality and diversity. Second, an E-DM nonlinear perturbation mechanism is embedded in temporary triangle-based search to develop the TriEDM multi-path strategy and enhance search capability. Third, Correlation-Guided Groupwise Orthogonal Learning (CGOL) leverages relationships among decision variables to improve search efficiency while reducing computational overhead. Fourth, an adaptive stagnation-aware Runge--Kutta correction is introduced to mitigate premature convergence. IWOO is evaluated on the IEEE CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017 benchmark suites against representative and high-performing optimizers, with ablation studies assessing the contribution of each strategy. Within the representative algorithm group, IWOO achieves Friedman ranks of 1.8000, 1.5833, and 1.4483 on CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017, respectively. Tests on six constrained engineering optimization problems further demonstrate its competitive accuracy, stability, and practical applicability.

articles.title: Duration-Aware World Models for Sleep Staging with Dwell-Time Constraints
articles.summary: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current…
articles.abstract: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current stage has persisted for its minimum duration. Discriminative classifiers fragment stage trajectories---for example, a 30 s Wake segment inside a 10 min N2 run---and even hidden semi-Markov smoothing leaves 11.3% of segments below the minimum dwell threshold. This paper presents a world model in which a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns dwell structure endogenously from EEG, via duration-aware latent sampling, a survival-curve dwell prior, and transition-matrix calibration, and a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer guarantees the minimum dwell at decoding. On SHHS-1 (200 subjects, 160/20/20, three repeated splits), the model reaches a test accuracy of 0.690 +/- 0.053 (95% CI over 3 folds) versus 0.641 +/- 0.042 for an identically split discriminative baseline, with macro-F1 +17.5 pp and better accuracy on all three folds. On Sleep-EDF the constraint layer cuts below-threshold segments from 71.8% to 0.1% with no accuracy loss (0.734 to 0.737), and an online locked scheduler reduces RL policy switches by 87% per night while keeping every policy run at least 90 s. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first system to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

articles.title: Controlling the latency in temporal coded spiking models for neuromorphic datasets
articles.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, where response time, or latency, matters as much as energy for real-time applications.…
articles.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, where response time, or latency, matters as much as energy for real-time applications. Time-to-first-spike (TTFS) coding with learnable synaptic delays is a natural way to exploit the timing of events. However, in state-of-the-art spiking neuron models, spike times emerge from nonlinear membrane dynamics and thresholds: no closed-form expression links network parameters to spike times, so latency can only be measured empirically, not specified or guaranteed at design time. Moreover, TTFS models are mostly evaluated on static datasets, which hides their latency on truly temporal data. Our hypothesis is that, if spike times are computed directly as closed-form functions of presynaptic spike times and synaptic delays, bypassing membrane potential and thresholding, latency becomes an explicit function of the learnable parameters that can be bounded, and therefore controlled, analytically. We build on this hypothesis with the Delay Neural Network (DeNN) in real time, which turns event streams into successive single-spike images, computes each spike time from standardised inter-spike intervals and synaptic delays, and links successive images through a long-term memory. We prove lower and upper bounds on the latency of every neuron of a layer, and show that bounding the synaptic parameters after training with a single hyperparameter places the latency anywhere between these bounds, without retraining. On a ten-class subset of the Google Speech Commands dataset, this post-training control exposes the accuracy--latency trade-off: a three-hidden-layer network reaches 94.25\% accuracy while deciding, on average, 477~ms after the end of the one-second input, and about 250~ms with confidence-based early decisions. Learning is also shown to concentrate the long-term memory on a few neurons. Latency thus becomes a design parameter of spiking models rather than a quantity measured after the fact, a step towards neuromorphic systems with real-time guarantees.

articles.title: When the implementation matters more than the algorithm: NSGA-II and other multi-objective optimizers in engineering design tools
articles.summary: Engineering design tools increasingly embed optimizers as ready-made components that users select by algorithm name, while operator settings and bound, integer and duplicate handling stay fixed…
articles.abstract: Engineering design tools increasingly embed optimizers as ready-made components that users select by algorithm name, while operator settings and bound, integer and duplicate handling stay fixed inside each tool. This study tests whether the name predicts the result. A tool-agnostic harness exposes one deterministic black box, an emulator of a published 22-variable mixed-integer building-performance problem, to the native optimizers of three Grasshopper plug-ins, to canonical NSGA-II, SMS-EMOA and GDE3 from Python libraries, and to the model-based RBFMOpt. Eighteen configurations were run at 5,000 evaluations under three population allocations, with statistics fixed in advance. Four NSGA-II implementations differed by up to 5% in hypervolume, more than three canonical algorithms of different families differed from one another, and their response to population size differed by up to 10 percentage points; for two MOEA/D implementations, by 28. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.

articles.title: Design and Analysis of Temporal Representations in Neural Networks
articles.summary: Neural networks, spiking or not, compute with amplitudes: activation values, spike counts, firing rates, never event times. No measure exists of how much a network uses time.
articles.abstract: Neural networks, spiking or not, compute with amplitudes: activation values, spike counts, firing rates, never event times. No measure exists of how much a network uses time. We propose one, the degree of temporal representation: the fraction of a network's four functions (encoding, activation, decoding, learning) whose variables or parameters are temporal, and hypothesise that it predicts performance on temporal tasks. At fixed architecture, accuracy and energy efficiency increase with the degree: a delay network of maximal degree reaches 98.94\% on Google Speech Commands with 175k parameters, above transformers. To test whether networks of different degree really differ, we convert the delay network into artificial and spiking networks with the same inputs and outputs. From this common start, the artificial one learns differently and temporal gradients depend on event times. Hence we obtain a design rule: for temporal data, make event times variables of a network's functions. Spiking networks, converted after training, keep the delay network's accuracy, unreachable by spiking networks trained from scratch.

articles.title: A Time-Variant Spiking Neuron from a Unified State-Dynamics Perspective
articles.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have increasingly incorporated rich neuronal dynamics to enhance temporal processing. However, richer dynamics do not necessarily enable neurons to adapt how…
articles.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) have increasingly incorporated rich neuronal dynamics to enhance temporal processing. However, richer dynamics do not necessarily enable neurons to adapt how information is processed over time. To examine this issue systematically, we introduce a unified state-dynamics framework that characterizes diverse spiking neurons through a common formulation and enables direct comparison of their dynamical designs. The framework reveals a common limitation of existing neurons: although they enhance temporal processing through richer internal states and state evolution, the dynamical rules determining how inputs are integrated, how states evolve, and how they are read out generally remain unchanged throughout temporal processing. Such time-invariant rules limit the ability of neurons to adjust information processing as information relevance changes over time. Inspired by time-varying regulation in biological neurons, we propose the Time-Variant Multi-Compartment Neuron (TV-MCN). TV-MCN builds on multiscale compartment dynamics and makes the rules for input integration, state evolution, and state readout time-varying according to the current input. Specifically, an input-dependent internal time regulates the rate of state evolution, while the current input dynamically modulates input integration and state readout. Extensive experiments show that TV-MCN achieves strong overall performance, with particularly large gains on tasks requiring selective retention and retrieval of information, while ablation studies further support the effectiveness of its time-varying mechanisms.

articles.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
articles.summary: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation.
articles.abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

articles.title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
articles.summary: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays…
articles.abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.

articles.title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
articles.summary: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens.
articles.abstract: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.

articles.title: Same Function, Different Trajectory: No Standard Optimizer Is Equivariant to Transformer Reparameterization
articles.summary: We show that two Transformers representing the same function can follow different training trajectories. For example, doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix preserves the model's function…
articles.abstract: We show that two Transformers representing the same function can follow different training trajectories. For example, doubling a query matrix and halving its key matrix preserves the model's function but changes the gradient scales seen by the optimizer. Our theoretical analysis establishes that standard block-local first-order optimizers fail to scale updates with parameters under a shared learning rate. For AdamW, transforming the first- and second-moment estimates alone does not correct the mismatch between parameter and update scales. To make runs restarted from equivalent checkpoints follow the same trajectory, we balance matrix pairs and transform their moment estimates together, bringing distinct but equivalent training states to the same starting point. To correct scale imbalance between paired Transformer matrices without changing predictions, we propose Symmetry-Aware Gradient Geometry Stabilization (SAGGS), which periodically equalizes the Frobenius norms of exact symmetry pairs, and its damped variant, Soft SAGGS. SAGGS reduces perplexity (PPL) by $0.374\pm0.026$ at 101M parameters on WikiText-103, and Soft SAGGS reduces PPL by $0.780\pm0.040$ in a 31M modern-architecture replication, both under scale imbalance. In a 123.8M checkpoint-resume experiment, reciprocally rescaling matrix pairs barely changes validation loss at restart but increases final PPL by $3.78\pm0.42$; hard and soft rebalancing recover to within $0.02$ PPL of the control.

articles.title: Saliency-Guided Replay for Continual Learning in Deep Spiking Neural Networks
articles.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates…
articles.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient neuromorphic computing, but they still suffer from catastrophic forgetting when learning tasks sequentially. This work investigates the integration of Experience Packing and Replay (EPR) as a memory-efficient continual learning strategy for deep SNNs under low-latency constraints. The proposed framework combines Batch Normalization Through Time stabilized VGG9 SNNs with Spike Activation Maps (SAM), which provide forward-only explanations based on spike activity. These explanations are temporally aggregated into spatial attention maps and used to select the most informative image patches for replay, instead of storing full images. Experiments on Split CIFAR10 and Split CIFAR100 show that SAM-guided EPR improves the accuracy-memory trade-off under tight memory budgets, and remains competitive while requiring substantially less storage.

articles.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
articles.summary: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms…
articles.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

articles.title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
articles.summary: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group…
articles.abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

articles.title: FidLIF: Parallel Training of High-Fidelity Spiking Neurons with Exact BPTT
articles.summary: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their…
articles.abstract: Although spiking neural networks (SNNs) show promise in energy-efficient computing through event-driven computation and stateful temporal processing, their recurrent membrane dynamics render their training inherently sequential and inefficient for long sequences. Existing methods achieve full-sequence parallelism in SNNs through two main strategies: redesigning or approximating spiking dynamics to avoid reset-coupled temporal dependencies, or relying on iterative relaxed fixed-point solvers that suffer from excessive memory costs and iteration-dependent backward overhead. To address these limitations, we present FidLIF, a novel framework that reconciles the incremental update and hard-reset behavior of standard spiking LIF neurons with parallel forward propagation and BPTT-equivalent backward propagation. FidLIF iteratively recovers the full-sequence membrane-potential trajectory in parallel. By exploiting the lower bidiagonal structure induced by the local recurrence of LIF neurons, FidLIF formulates each forward trajectory correction and backward adjoint propagation as associative scans with an $O(\log T)$ temporal depth. This formulation also supports input-dependent neuronal parameters and allows the same neuron to perform full-sequence parallel training and incremental step-by-step inference at deployment. In our numerical convergence evaluation, FidLIF achieves a mean absolute error below $10^{-7}$ relative to the matched serial relaxed LIF dynamics, while yielding gradients numerically equivalent to exact BPTT. Our Triton implementation delivers favorable long-sequence latency and memory scaling, while achieving competitive performance on four sequential classification benchmarks. By reconciling parallel training with step-by-step execution, FidLIF enables high-fidelity spiking dynamics to benefit from parallel hardware without compromising incremental inference at deployment.

articles.title: Time Window Optimization for Motor Imagery Classification via Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window…
articles.abstract: Online motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) typically decode continuous EEG using fixed-length sliding windows that may be misaligned with neural events. Existing window optimization methods often evaluate windows independently, overlooking temporal dependencies and potentially producing fragmented or physiologically implausible selections. We propose Temporal Structure Embedded Reinforcement Learning (TSE-RL), a framework that incorporates prior knowledge of MI event structure into a constrained Markov decision process for adaptive window optimization. First, TSE-RL assigns each window an explicit semantic role through Discard, Onset, Sustain, or Offset actions, extending binary retain/discard decisions to event-level alignment. Second, a finite-state machine masks invalid actions to enforce the temporal order of MI phases and promote physiologically plausible window sequences. Third, a Transformer-based history encoder captures dependencies across windows, improving training stability and computational efficiency compared with recurrent architectures. TSE-RL is plug-and-play and can be integrated with diverse MI classifiers. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in decoding performance in both cross-session and cross-subject settings. Visualization analyses further suggest that the learned window selection policy aligns with neurophysiological principles.

articles.title: DTA-GT: Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer for Neural Network Representation Learning
articles.summary: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled…
articles.abstract: Architecture attribute predictors reduce the cost of neural architecture search by estimating accuracy or latency from a small set of evaluated candidates. Neural architectures are operation-labeled directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where edge directions determine computational roles and execution dependencies. Existing graph Transformer predictors incorporate topological and directional information in different ways, but primarily focus on specific mechanisms rather than coordinated encoder-wide modeling of these semantics. We introduce encoder-wide directional consistency, a design principle that coordinates the modeling of directed computational semantics across node initialization, global spectral encoding, pairwise interaction, and feature updates. To implement this principle, we propose DTA-GT, a Direction- and Topology-Aware Graph Transformer that integrates direction- and topology-aware node initialization, magnetic Laplacian spectral encoding, direction-dual structural attention, and a Direction-Sensitive MoE-FFN. Across accuracy and latency prediction on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, DTA-GT consistently outperforms representative RNN-, CNN-, GNN-, Transformer-, and hybrid predictors under limited-budget settings. Ablations and magnetic spectral controls support the contribution of the direction-aware stages and orientation-sensitive spectral information, while mechanistic diagnostics characterize module behavior. These results support encoder-wide directional consistency as an effective design principle for architecture DAG representation.

articles.title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation
